name: Felix the governor
charge: Trembling at the judgment to come, hoping for a bribe, and leaving a man he knew to be innocent bound
summary: Felix already had a more perfect knowledge of that way when he deferred the hearing (Acts 24:22). He sent for Paul with his wife Drusilla, and as Paul reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, the governor trembled and put him off to a convenient season (Acts 24:24-25). He sent for him often afterwards, hoping money would be given him, and after two years he left Paul bound to do the Jews a pleasure (Acts 24:26-27). No repentance and no sentence upon Felix is recorded.
offenseFull: The record says Felix had more perfect knowledge of that way before he deferred the case (Acts 24:22). That is the key to the man. The liar knows the lie he told: he knew exactly what Paul was teaching, which is why the preaching reached him. He came with his wife Drusilla, called a Jewess; she was the daughter of Herod Agrippa, of the stock of Edom, converted in generations earlier, and she is the living example of what Christ afterwards named, the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews and are not (Acts 24:24; Revelation 2:9). Paul reasoned of righteousness, which is the commandments, of temperance, and of judgment to come, and Felix trembled (Acts 24:25). Trembling is not faith. The devils also believe, and tremble (James 2:19). And if what Paul preached had been nonsense, a Roman governor would have laughed at him instead of shaking.

He put the preacher off to a convenient season, then sent for him the oftener, hoping that money would be given him to loose Paul (Acts 24:25-26). The law forbids the gift outright, because the gift blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19), and he that justifies the wicked and condemns the just is an abomination to the Lord (Proverbs 17:15). The histories place him exactly. Judea had been annexed and put under procurators who tampered with the high priesthood, beheaded the men they called false prophets, and crucified the sons of Judas the Galilean. Felix was the newest of them and was guilty of fanning the hatred of the growing zealot camp by his harsh handling of every discontent, until the daggermen stepped up their own resistance and began assassinating the sympathizers of Rome, the corrupt high priest Jonathan among them. A governor who tried both to frighten a nation and to sell its prisoners was hurrying his province toward 70 AD.
judgmentFull: After two years Porcius Festus came into his room, and Felix, willing to show the Jews a pleasure, left Paul bound (Acts 24:27). There is no divine sentence carried out on him in the book and no repentance either. There is only the list of his acts: postponement, the hope of a payment, and a last concession to political favour at the prisoner’s expense. The convenient season never came, and the accepted time and the day of salvation are now (2 Corinthians 6:2).

The warning in the case is for the hearer. A man can hear this gospel repeatedly, know in himself that it is true, shake while he hears it, and still hand the preacher back to the men who want him dead. Fear of judgment is not obedience. And the same evidence that convicted Felix convicts the men who spend money and airtime fighting the teaching now: if the work were of men it would come to nothing on its own, and Gamaliel’s counsel was to leave it alone, lest they be found fighting against God (Acts 5:38-39). Nobody goes to that expense over something they believe is nothing.

text.text: And when Felix heard these things, having more perfect knowledge of that way, he deferred them, and said, When Lysias the chief captain shall come down, I will know the uttermost of your matter.
And after certain days, when Felix came with his wife Drusilla, which was a Jewess, he sent for Paul, and heard him concerning the faith in Christ.
And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee.
I know thy works, and tribulation, and poverty, (but thou art rich) and I know the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.
Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.
He hoped also that money should have been given him of Paul, that he might loose him: wherefore he sent for him the oftener, and communed with him.
But after two years Porcius Festus came into Felix’ room: and Felix, willing to shew the Jews a pleasure, left Paul bound.
And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous.
Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.
He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the Lord.
(For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)
And now I say unto you, Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought:
But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God.
